title: ChatGD: Learnings (So Far) from our Legal GenAI Experiment
pub: LinkedIn Pulse (Gunderson Dettmer chief innovation officer, first-person)
author: Joe Green

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: Green accepts selective, supervised experimentation rather than broad substitution and adds a concrete adoption model: mandatory training, collaborative use-case discovery, and explicit task boundaries. The account strengthens the cluster’s implementation case but provides no measured evidence of reliability or productivity gains.
qs: We framed the rollout of ChatGD as a collaborative experiment designed to help everyone move up the learning curve and to crowdsource the most promising use cases and methods for getting the best results out of GenAI-powered tools.

We also shared ideal use cases for GenAI (e.g., text manipulation) and areas where we thought the technology was not well suited for use without further advancements (e.g., search engine replacement).

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, human-led deployment by documenting attorney use on bounded retrieval, summarisation, drafting and ideation tasks, alongside training, RAG infrastructure and deliberate model choices. It provides an early implementation case rather than evidence of general legal competence, realised productivity or effective verification, so its support is practical but limited.
qs: Our attorneys are using it to retrieve and manipulate or summarize language in legal agreements, draft and change the tone of emails, summarize documents and articles, and brainstorm different examples of legal language or topics for presentations.

We largely attribute the cost-effectiveness of ChatGD to two strategic decisions: (1) self-hosting an open-source model for RAG vector embeddings and (2) leveraging GPT 3.5 Turbo for both pure chat and RAG functionalities instead of using the most expensive models available.

kp.k: Internal rollout combines mandatory training with collaborative experimentation
kp.d: Green reports that Gunderson Dettmer launched its homegrown RAG-enabled ChatGD application in August 2023 after a summer beta test. Access required initial training, delivered live or on demand, with three live sessions tailored to attorneys, paralegals and business professionals. More than half the firm attended a live session. Training addressed underlying technology, safe and ethical use, suitable tasks and limitations; the rollout sought to build familiarity and crowdsource effective uses.
qs: As a prerequisite to using ChatGD, we required users to complete an initial training (either live or on demand).

We framed the rollout of ChatGD as a collaborative experiment designed to help everyone move up the learning curve and to crowdsource the most promising use cases and methods for getting the best results out of GenAI-powered tools.

We also shared ideal use cases for GenAI (e.g., text manipulation) and areas where we thought the technology was not well suited for use without further advancements (e.g., search engine replacement).
More than half of the entire firm attended one of those three trainings in real time, which is a testament to the incredible level of interest in GenAI and the tool we built.

kp.k: Early usage data show broad uptake, predominantly ordinary chat
kp.d: Writing four months after launch, Green reports internal usage data showing nearly half the firm had used ChatGD, with steadily increasing usage and more than nine thousand completed prompts across several thousand conversation threads. Users had uploaded hundreds of document collections for RAG; RAG interactions accounted for more than 10% of total interactions. These are reported adoption and activity measures, rather than measured improvements in work quality or productivity.
qs: Nearly half of the firm has already used ChatGD.
Usage has been steadily increasing, with more than nine thousand prompts submitted and completed across several thousand conversation threads.

We have created vector search indices for hundreds of document collections uploaded by our users for RAG, and prompts leveraging the advanced RAG feature accounted for more than 10% of the total volume of interactions with the tool.

kp.k: Low projected costs depend on deliberate model choices
kp.d: Green projects annual out-of-pocket costs below $10,000 for providing ChatGD across the firm, describing this as low relative to enterprise alternatives. This is a projection rather than a completed annual expenditure figure. He attributes cost-effectiveness largely to self-hosted open-source embedding technology and using GPT 3.5 Turbo rather than the most expensive models for both ordinary chat and RAG.
qs: We project the total annual out-of-pocket cost for providing ChatGD to our entire firm will be less than $10,000—a staggeringly low figure, especially when compared to the alternatives currently available in the enterprise market.

We largely attribute the cost-effectiveness of ChatGD to two strategic decisions: (1) self-hosting an open-source model for RAG vector embeddings and (2) leveraging GPT 3.5 Turbo for both pure chat and RAG functionalities instead of using the most expensive models available.

kp.k: Lawyers use AI for language-intensive assistance
kp.d: Green reports attorneys using ChatGD to retrieve, manipulate and summarize agreement language, draft emails and adjust tone, summarize documents and articles, and brainstorm legal language and presentation topics. Users also enlist the model to improve their prompting. The account describes assistance with existing lawyer tasks, without reporting quantified time savings or changes to staffing.
qs: Our attorneys are using it to retrieve and manipulate or summarize language in legal agreements, draft and change the tone of emails, summarize documents and articles, and brainstorm different examples of legal language or topics for presentations.
They have discovered creative ways to have the LLM help teach them to craft better prompts.

kp.k: Business professionals apply AI across firm support functions
kp.d: The reported applications extend beyond attorneys: business and technology professionals use ChatGD for marketing content, RFP responses, meeting preparation, data structuring and formatting, coding, and written communications. Green presents these as current uses within the firm rather than predictions about future roles.
qs: Our business and technology professionals have used the tool to help them create and repurpose content for marketing, answer RFPs, prepare for meetings, structure and format data, write code and improve their written communications.

kp.k: User feedback connects limitations, training and tool development
kp.d: Green describes in-app crowdsourced feedback as a mechanism for identifying both useful applications and poorly performing tasks. The firm uses examples of poor performance to teach technological limitations, improve prompting and guide tool improvements. Tackling more complex use cases remains a future ambition conditional on technological improvement.
qs: Our users have also been providing great crowdsourced feedback directly within the app to help us identify good use cases to share with the rest of the firm, as well as use cases where the technology does not perform as well.

We use the latter for training users on the limitations of GenAI technology, teaching them how to write better prompts to get better results and identifying how we can improve the tool as the technology improves so that we can tackle more complex use cases in the future.

kp.k: Task-specific retrieval and model routing balance capability and cost
kp.d: Green reports newly released updates combining keyword search, knowledge graphs, vector embeddings and autonomous retrieval, with prompt routing selecting retrieval methods. The updated stack uses three foundational models, allocating larger models and context windows to summarization while retaining cheaper models for fact retrieval. Detailed summarization receives full source context where possible. A further fact-retrieval upgrade to GPT 4 Turbo is planned once production access becomes available, enabled by the model-agnostic architecture.
qs: Using prompt-routing and open source embeddings models, we have constructed multiple indices that employ a combination of keywords, knowledge graphs, vector embeddings and autonomous retrieval to dynamically optimize the chosen fact retrieval method for a user’s specific prompt as part of our RAG workflow.

This now includes routing prompts to different LLMs for fact retrieval and summarization to perform the language generation step of the RAG process, allowing us to use larger context windows and larger models for better summarization while reserving more cost-effective models for fact retrieval.

For especially detailed summarization tasks, we route these requests to our most powerful models with the largest context windows to provide the model with full context of the source material, where possible.
In brief, we are now using three different foundational models as part of the ChatGD tech stack, deploying the best available model for each particular purpose.
Moreover, we are ready to upgrade our fact retrieval LLM to GPT 4 Turbo as soon as it becomes available to us for production use, thanks to our model agnostic architecture.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Joe Green reports that ChatGD augments legal and business work through retrieval, text manipulation, summarization, drafting and brainstorming.
pts.d: Writing as Gunderson Dettmer’s chief innovation officer, Green describes actual internal uses rather than predicting lawyer replacement. Attorneys use ChatGD on agreement language, correspondence, documents and presentation preparation; business and technology staff use it for marketing, RFPs, meetings, data formatting, coding and communications. He characterizes these applications as helping colleagues work smarter, without quantifying time savings or improvements in work quality.

pts.k: Green claims that an internally built GenAI application can be provided firm-wide at a low projected out-of-pocket cost through specific model and infrastructure choices.
pts.d: Green projects annual out-of-pocket expenditure below $10,000 and describes this as low relative to enterprise alternatives. He attributes the economics principally to self-hosted open-source embeddings and use of GPT 3.5 Turbo rather than the most expensive models. This is a projection of out-of-pocket expenditure, not a reported fully loaded cost or a measured return on investment.

pts.k: Green presents task-specific model routing and retrieval methods as a way to improve internal legal-AI functionality while managing costs.
pts.d: Green reports newly released routing across retrieval methods and different LLMs, using larger models and context windows for summarization and cheaper models for fact retrieval. He describes a three-model, model-agnostic architecture that permits future upgrades. These are reported engineering changes and intended benefits, not benchmarked improvements in legal accuracy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of first-person implementation experience, internal usage data and crowdsourced user feedback.
pts.d: Green reports nearly half of the firm having used ChatGD, more than nine thousand prompts across several thousand threads, hundreds of uploaded document collections indexed for RAG, and RAG accounting for more than 10% of interactions. These figures support his account of adoption and engagement, while the use-case descriptions draw on colleagues’ experiences. The source does not provide controlled productivity measurements, accuracy benchmarks or a detailed enterprise-cost comparison.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account covers approximately four months after the August 2023 rollout and treats effective use as conditional on training, task suitability and continuing technical development.
pts.d: Green writes near the end of 2023, following a summer beta and August launch. Initial training was mandatory. He identifies text manipulation as suitable but regards search-engine replacement as unsuitable without further advances. More complex use cases remain a future objective. Detailed summarization receives full source context where possible, and the planned GPT 4 Turbo retrieval upgrade depends on production availability. The annual cost figure is prospective rather than a completed year’s expenditure.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are Gunderson Dettmer’s attorneys, paralegals, business professionals and technology staff.
pts.d: Green describes a firm-wide internal learning and workflow initiative. Attorneys receive assistance with legal language and communication; business and technology professionals receive assistance with operational and content tasks. Paralegals are explicitly included in training, although their distinct use cases are not specified. The firm bears the deployment costs and uses employee feedback to guide development. The source makes no concrete claim about client fee reductions, staffing displacement, access to justice or legal-market restructuring.
